title: Jesus' coming and the millennium
summary: A deeper look at the second coming: it will be visible, audible, glorious and global. It is accompanied by the resurrection of the righteous and the transformation of the living, and then a thousand years (the millennium) - the saved in heaven, an emptied earth, Satan bound, and judgment on the wicked.

items.comment: John announces the return of Jesus on the clouds, visible to all humanity. The coming will be seen by the whole world - not secret, not symbolic.

questions.text: Why does it matter that everyone will see Him - what does such universal visibility rule out?

items.comment: Jesus compares His return to lightning visible across the whole sky - open, sudden, impossible to miss. This is a safeguard against false, "quiet" comings.

questions.text: How does this image protect against rumors like "Christ has already secretly come here or there"?

items.comment: The coming is accompanied by the sound of a trumpet and angels gathering God's people from all over the earth. The event is audible, glorious and cosmic in scale.

questions.text: What does it say about the magnitude of this event that all of heaven takes part in it?

items.comment: The angels assure the disciples that Jesus will return in the same way they watched Him ascend into heaven - personally, visibly, bodily. The manner of His departure sets the manner of His return.

questions.text: Since Jesus will come back "in the same way," which ideas about His coming must be rejected?

items.comment: Jesus warns us not to believe those who will point to Christ hidden somewhere in the wilderness or in the inner rooms. The visibility and global scope of His coming is a shield against deception.

questions.text: By what - according to Jesus Himself - can you tell that a given "announcement of His coming" is false?

items.comment: Paul describes that at the return of Jesus the believing dead will rise first, and the living will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord. The Christian hope is resurrection at the coming, not the departure of souls beforehand.

questions.text: What comfort is there in the thought that being parted from those who died in Christ is temporary - until the day of His coming?

items.label: "being caught up / snatched away" (1 Thess 4:17)
items.content: The Greek verb in 1 Thess 4:17 (harpazo) means a sudden, forceful taking, a "catching up." The New Testament, however, knows nothing of a quiet, secret catching away: it happens at the sound of a trumpet, at the visible coming (Rev 1:7; Matt 24:27, 30-31). In the Bible, being caught up and the second coming are one event, not two separate phases. The Greek form is given cautiously - transliteration and meaning to be confirmed at review.

items.label: "the coming" as parousia, epiphaneia, apokalypsis
items.content: The New Testament describes the return of Jesus with three main words: parousia (coming, royal presence), epiphaneia (open appearing) and apokalypsis (unveiling). All three stress that the event will be open and perceptible, not hidden or merely spiritual - parousia refers directly to the solemn, visible arrival of a king. This is the linguistic foundation of the truth that His coming "every eye will see" (Rev 1:7). The Greek forms are given cautiously - to be confirmed at review.

items.comment: Paul announces that at the sound of the last trumpet all believers will be transformed in an instant. The mortal body will be changed in the blink of an eye - this is a moment, not a process.

questions.text: What does the promise mean to you that a weak, mortal body can be transformed in a single instant?

items.comment: What is mortal will be clothed with immortality, and death will at last be swallowed up in victory. The coming of Jesus is the day death is defeated.

questions.text: How do you live differently when you know that death is not the last word, but a defeated enemy?

items.comment: Jesus announces an hour in which all who rest in the graves will hear His voice and rise - some to life. It is His voice that wakes the dead, not their own immortality.

questions.text: What does it say about the power of Jesus that His voice alone brings the dead back to life?

items.label: two resurrections: "to life" and "to judgment"
items.content: Jesus' words about a "resurrection to life" and a "resurrection to judgment" (John 5:29) correspond to the two resurrections of Revelation 20. The "first resurrection" (Rev 20:5-6), at the second coming, is precisely the "resurrection to life" - all of God's faithful from the beginning of earth's history take part in it. "The rest of the dead" do not rise until after the thousand years (Rev 20:5). The coherence of these pictures (John 5; 1 Thess 4; Rev 20) to be confirmed at review.

items.comment: Paul calls the waiting for the appearing of the glory of Jesus the blessed hope of believers. For the believer, the coming is a hope, not a threat.

questions.text: Is the return of Jesus more of a "blessed hope" to you, or a source of fear - and why?

items.comment: The text speaks of the saved, who come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years, while the rest of the dead do not rise until the end of that period. There are therefore two resurrections, separated by the millennium.

questions.text: What does it mean that the first resurrection (of the righteous) and the second (of the rest) are a thousand years apart?

items.label: where the words "millennium" and "thousand years" come from
items.content: The term "millennium" comes from two Latin words: mille ("thousand") and annus ("year"), that is, "a thousand years." The phrase "a thousand years" itself appears in Revelation 20 six times (vv. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), and only here in all of Scripture is the teaching about the millennium stated outright. Interestingly, E. G. White distinguished the mistaken idea of an earthly "temporal millennium" from the biblical "thousand years" that the saved spend in heaven with Christ.

items.label: two resurrections and the structure of the millennium
items.content: Revelation 20 assumes TWO resurrections separated by a thousand years: the first - of the righteous, at the second coming (Rev 20:4-6; 1 Thess 4:16); the second - of the rest, after the millennium (Rev 20:5, 7-9). In this view it unfolds as follows: at the coming of Jesus the saved are taken to heaven, the wicked perish, the earth is left desolate (cf. Jer 4:23-26), and Satan is immobilized by having no one left to deceive. After the thousand years comes the resurrection and the final judgment on evil (developed in study 28). Coherence requires reading Rev 20 together with 1 Thess 4 and John 5:28-29 - to be confirmed at review.

items.comment: The one who shares in the first resurrection is called blessed, because the second death has no power over them. The saved spend the millennium with Christ, safe.

questions.text: What assurance is given by the promise that over the one who shares in the first resurrection "the second death has no power"?

items.comment: Satan is immobilized for a thousand years - he has no one left to deceive, because the wicked are dead and the saved are in heaven. His "binding" is being cut off from any activity on the desolate earth.

questions.text: What does it mean that "the binding of Satan" is the absence of victims to deceive, and not just a literal chain?

items.label: "the binding of Satan" as inactivity, not conversion (Rev 20:1-3)
items.content: Satan's immobilization for a thousand years does not mean his reform or salvation, but enforced inactivity: on the desolate earth there is no longer anyone left for him to deceive (the saved are in heaven, the wicked are dead). Revelation gives him four names - the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan - the same as in Rev 12:7-9. Because he is a spiritual being, the "key" and "chain" are also symbolic: they are the circumstances that take away his field of action. This is not a second chance for evil, but its isolation before the final judgment.

items.label: "the abyss" (abyssos) as a state of chaos and emptiness
items.content: The Greek abyssos ("abyss," "bottomless deep"), into which Satan is cast (Rev 20:1, 3), is the same word the Septuagint uses in Gen 1:2 for the earth that was "formless and empty" before creation. The image speaks, then, not so much of a literal dungeon as of a state of desolation: after the coming of Jesus the earth returns to chaos, and Satan is imprisoned on it, unable to do anything creative or organized. It is a striking picture of the utter powerlessness of evil.

items.comment: The prophet sees the earth empty and formless, void of people - a picture of desolation reminiscent of the state before creation. This fits the desolate earth during the millennium.

questions.text: How does this image of a desolate earth help us understand where life is NOT taking place during the thousand years?

items.comment: Paul reminds us that it is the saints who will judge the world. During the millennium the saved take part in reviewing God's verdicts - the judgment is open and just, not arbitrary.

questions.text: Why is it good that the saved can "review" God's verdicts before the final judgment is rendered?

items.label: why a judgment by the saved, if the outcome is already settled?
items.content: Since people's destinies are already settled at the second coming, the judgment by the saved during the millennium (Rev 20:4; 1 Cor 6:2-3) does not determine the verdicts, but serves to understand and confirm them. Given the cosmic dimension of the problem of sin (Job 1-2; Eph 3:10), the whole universe - the redeemed, the angels, beings from unfallen worlds - is to be assured that God acted justly. It is also an answer to the pain of the redeemed who ask about the fate of loved ones: the judgment gives full clarity about God's character.

items.comment: After the thousand years Satan is released, the wicked rise (the second resurrection), but their final rebellion ends in judgment. The millennium closes the great controversy.

questions.text: What does it mean that even the final rebellion does not take God by surprise, but leads to the just end of evil?

items.label: "Gog and Magog" as an image of universal rebellion
items.content: "Gog and Magog" in Rev 20:8 are not the names of particular nations or modern states, but a symbol of universal rebellion against God (cf. Ezek 38:2). The number of the rebels "like the sand of the sea" stresses the vastness, but also the futility, of this final attack on "the beloved city" (the New Jerusalem). The fact that the wicked, immediately after their resurrection, turn against God once again confirms the rightness of God's earlier verdict.

items.label: "the great white throne" and "the second death" (Rev 20:11-15)
items.content: After the millennium comes the judgment at "the great white throne" (Rev 20:11-15): the books are opened, and the wicked are judged according to their deeds. "The second death," identified with "the lake of fire," is a final and irreversible death, not eternal torment - a human being is not by nature immortal, and so is consumed (cf. Mal 4:1; Matt 10:28). Even Satan's punishment has an end, because he too is a created being. The result is eternal, but the action of the fire itself comes to an end - and from the ashes God creates a new earth (2 Pet 3:13).

items.label: "devoured / consumed" (katesthio) and the end of evil
items.content: In Rev 20:9 the wicked are "devoured" by fire - the Greek verb (katesthio, "to consume, to devour") points to complete annihilation, not to unending suffering. The same happens to death and the realm of the dead (Hades), thrown into the lake of fire (Rev 20:14): not only sin is removed, but death itself. Hence the promise that there will be no more tears, death or pain (Rev 21:4). The Greek form is given cautiously - to be confirmed at review.

application.text: The second coming is not a vague idea or a private experience - it will be visible, audible and global, perceptible to every person. For the believer it is a blessed hope: the day when the dead in Christ will rise, the living will be transformed, and death will be defeated. Then a thousand years with Christ - safe, taking part in an open, just judgment, while evil is isolated. The great controversy moves toward an end in which God not only triumphs but also explains everything. This is a hope that puts life in order today.
application.challenge: This week read 1 Thess 4:16-18 and notice that Paul ends this passage with a call to comfort one another with these words. If you have lost someone who trusted Jesus, use this promise as comfort. Write down too one question you would like to understand during the millennium - and entrust it to the God who is just.
